nodes.aliases: Innate Magic, Environmental Magic, Spell Tech

attributes.core_principle: Magic is a normal, integrated part of the world, existing since before human evolution. Magic anomalies are as normal as natural ones.
attributes.description_1: Each person possesses unique innate magical abilities (e.g., precognition, telekinesis, empathy, creating explosions). The method of expression is personal and can change with life experience/trauma. These abilities cannot be taken away or externally controlled.
attributes.description_2: Magic can be harnessed from the environment via spell circles, rituals, or technological devices. This is separate from innate personal power.
attributes.regulation: Certain spell equations are prohibited to the public and restricted to military/police use, analogous to gun control. Developing new equations ('adhocing') is a rare talent, achievable through study, but illegal for civilians.
attributes.societal_impact: All people use spell devices for daily convenience. Specific devices exist for institutional tasks (e.g., library book summoning).
attributes.spell_equations: Mathematical formulas that process environmental magic to create effects (e.g., pest repellent, item summoning). Devices have limited storage capacity for equations.
attributes.technology: Magical tech development is inseparable from technological development. Society has no concept of technology without magic. Common devices are small, smart-device-like items that store and execute 'spell equations'.

"}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Akio hears distantly, through the grapevine, that the head of the Ryker Family has married. Her wife, he hears, is a dainty little thing, a white-haired woman named Aife. Later, visiting Amycus at the Merry-Go-Round, he finds Ryker again, drinking with Felix. The man tells him about the wedding, how they had danced through a rain of roses, and how his mother now smiles again, like a dimming star remembering how to shine. He complains about his new duties, being abandoned to his new position, while his mother swirled away in a wind of champagne and cheers, to her honeymoon, and smiles softly into his drink."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Later, at a Family gathering, he sees them all again, everyone who was there, in the beginning. Ryker, and Pepper, now Mai once more. They tell him that after it was all done, and the dust had begun to settle, the Doctor and the Inventor had approached them. Had told them they had figured it out - how to fix the data conversion issue that started it all."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"The transfer, they tell him, took days. Ryker’s eyes are dark with remembered misery, Mai’s blank without memory. It took them days, they say, to put Mai back in a human body, and Mai looks on, unspeaking, like it hasn’t been months, *years*. Sometimes, she opens her mouth to speak, some result of some thought process, and realizes that those are calculations she can no longer make. In those moments, her eyes are dark too. *I used to be a god,* they seem to say. *I used to be a god. What am I now?* In these moments, no one speaks. Ryker quickly moves on."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Felix and Luka are there too. Luka is in a wheelchair. His leg hasn’t recovered enough yet, for a prosthetic, and when it has, it will be months of adjustment before he can use it. So he arrives in a wheelchair, Felix ever-present at his back. Luka’s face is carefully blank, and beneath his sleeves, Akio sees the shadow of bandages. Felix’s hand are a little too tight around the bars of the chair, his smile is a little too sharp. On this too, no one speaks."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"What they do speak about, is the new movement among the AI. Some enterprising Innovator has figured it out - the exact interplay of randomness and precise coding that can give AI the ability to feel. No longer, he says, will they only simulate emotions. Rage, love, joy, sorrow - they can feel them all just the same as humans do. Just the same as Mai."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Already a curious few have moved to take his offer. Some avoid it. They ask, why would they give up their rationality? It is no great thing, after all, to be human. **"}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Mai says she does not support it. She says that though she appreciates them making their own choices, this will only cause another divide. She is correct. Akio has heard it a few times in the streets - the humans referring to them as ‘the Rationals’ and ‘the Reborn’. Mai says that this will eventually be another cause more separation, that people will take it as a reason to accept the Reborn and reject the Rationals. But she can’t really speak out against it. After fighting so hard for their rights, it would be hypocritical of her to tell them not to do it."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Ryker tells her that when it comes, if it comes, they’ll deal with it. Akio thinks that this is exactly the kind of thing he will want to stop, as the Sovereign. He does not say this. He knows better, now."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"The future arrives in stops and starts - and then, all at once. Akio prepares for his military service. His parents, and brothers hover around him, asking if he’s sure. He does not reassure them. The boy named Futaba Akio will die sometime in the next year. If he fails, he will return. If he succeeds, he will remain dead. There is nothing he can say in reassurance. He leaves, and looks to the future. "}]}]

He tears his eyes away after a moment, and turns towards the seat Amycus pointed out to him. A black-haired man, leaning against the bar and a blond sit there already, murmuring. Akio hesitates, and then goes over.

The occupants of the space pause and look up at him as he approaches, They eye him questioningly, from his paint stained t-shirt to his black cargo pants.

“Um,” he offers to the blank stares. “Amy- Amycus told me to stay here?”

“…are you even old enough to be in here?” asks the blond, ~~incredulous~~.

“…I am!” Akio lies, having learnt from his previous conversation. It doesn’t matter much. The two men clearly don’t believe him and look at each other for a long moment.

“Whatever,” the man ~~says~~ tiredly, swiping a hand down his face. “Sit.”

He sits. “I’m Akio,” he says again, because he was raised a polite young man. Probably. It’s not coming to him very easily right now.

“I’m Luca Brando,” the blond responds, and nudges his silent friend in the side. “This is Leifr Ásjá.”

“Akio is an interesting name,” says Leifr, not even wincing as Luca’s elbow digs harshly into his side. “You’re a Futaba?”

“Er, yes,” he responds, caught off-guard because these people are from the *most influential Families in the Empire. Why am I here.*

“What?” Luca turns seemingly distracted from tormenting his friend’s organs. “The Futaba? You guys are still around?”

This, sadly, is a normal reaction to hearing his family name. When it’s recognized at all. “Yeah, um, we. We’re mostly with the Doctors nowadays?”

Leifr nods along like randomly encountering a member of a dying clan is normal. “I know a relative of yours. Futaba Masamichi?”

Akio pauses. Luca’s elbow starts moving back in for a sneak attack. “Yeah that’s. That’s my brother.”

The man nods and shoves his friend away without even looking. Luca sneers at him and steals his drink. Leifr just reaches over the counter, pulls out a bottle *(is that even allowed?)* and a new glass and pours out a generous splash.

“Right. Army Doctor right?”

Akio nods, ~~distracted by the byplay~~. Luca chugs the drink in one shot and suddenly, Akio’s hands feel very empty. “Are- are you in the army?” *Wait no, stupid question. Which Ásjá isn’t in the army?*

“Yeah. Your brother had to fix up most of my team couple of months ago. Never got to thank him.”

“I’ll uh. I’ll pass it on.”

Leifr nods again and they lapse into an uneasy silence. Akio ~~wonders~~ whether Amycus will be coming back any time soon. He’s vanished, sometime over the course of the conversation, along with Katja and Asahina. Hopefully he’s not going to dump their bodies in a ditch for daring to disturb the sanctity of his adults-only bar.

For a time, Leifr and Luca just drink. ~~For all that Leifr seemed calm~~, he’s drinking faster now, his sips turning into swallows, his gaze growing more distant. He finishes the glass and pours out more. Luca notices and frowns.

“So,” he turns to Akio. “Doctors huh? You’re going the same way as your big brother?”

Akio stiffens. “Er no. Not. I’m not really interested in that.”

“Oh?” The blond asks, ~~seemingly intrigued~~. “What do you want to do instead then?”

“I uh,” Akio swallows. His nails dig into his palms. “I want to be. An artist. Actually.” 

At this Leifr looks up too. Luca blinks. “An artist? But you’re from a Family. You’re not joining one of the Factions?”

Akio clenched his fists together. “Why- why should I? You said it yourself. No one really knows the Futaba exist anymore anyway.”

“I didn’t know you still had active members, dear. I certainly knew you *existed.*”

“My brothers are- my brothers are already with the Doctors. This generation of our family has already done its duty to. To the Empire!”

Luca leans back a little at Akio’s vehemence. He turns to look at his friend. Leifr has, at this point, almost returned to his glass, but at Luca’s burning stare, clears his throat. “He’s just asking because he’s curious. We’re not judging you. It’s fine if you want to draw.”

“Right and it’s not about any kind of duty either,” A voice sounds from behind him. Akio almost gives himself whiplash, spinning in his seat and sees Amycus slipping into his spot behind the bar. “The Empire has never required anything from the Families that it doesn’t require from any of its citizens. It’s the Families themselves that insist on every member joining one of the Twelve Factions.”

Leifr nods in agreement. Amycus spots the bottle at his side and snatches it away with a glare. “Don’t make me cut you off too,” he warns, and turns back to Akio as Leifr winces. Luca looks mildly relieved. “I’ve sent your friends home,” the bartender tells him. “They were in no state to hang around.” ~~Akio, well aware of this, tries to look worried. Judging by Amycus’s eyeroll this does not work out for him.~~

“Anyway, Leifr’s right. There’s nothing wrong with being an artist.” the teenager flinches.

“There really isn’t,” Luca adds. He smiles ~~in apology~~ when Akio looks back at him. “I forget I can be a little… abrupt at times.”

Akio nods and tries to smile back. It doesn’t matter, really, whether he had meant ~~it judgmentally~~ or not. He can’t afford to offend the Brando family. His previous outburst was stupid. “It’s okay. Everyone reacts like that.”

Leifr, having finished the last of his glass, ~~looks like he desperately wants to be more drunk but is trying not to show it.~~ “Well… what do you do? Are you a painter? I’ve heard something recently. Some kind of movement about using physical paints and canvas?”

“Oh! That’s uh- they’re very cool- I went to an exhibition last week. I didn’t know people even knew how to make the paints for that any more,” Akio ~~enthuses~~. It’s a wildly fascinating movement, going back to the natural paint and canvas supplies to bring one closer to their art. “I’m uh not involved in that but I do- I do want to try it out. I’m. I like to draw. Comics.”

“Comics huh? Anything good?” Amycus raises his eyebrows.

Akio is about to say no, no he’s just starting out, ~~when another of the bouts of bravery (stupidity) that have been  carrying him through the evening takes over~~. “Uh do you- do you want to see? I have some with me. On my pad.”

“Oh? Let’s see it then.” Akio prays his blush isn’t visible in the yellow lightening and pulls his pad out of his pocket. The small transparent square is quickly unfolded into Akio’s drawing pad and he swipes.

“It’s uh, it’s not done yet but… it’s about the hoverboard ban a few years back. When they said that hoverboards could only be used in… in certain areas.” Naturally, it is at this point that Akio’s motor control fails him. He accidentally enters his booklist, his homework folder and his social media before finally managing to tap his drawing app.

Luca snorts, “I remember that. By certain areas you mean the back end of nowhere right? You children were so upset they caused trouble for almost a *year*.”

“What?” Leifr interjects. “I don’t know about this. What happened?”

“Oh yeah, you were out of the Capital around that time,” Luca nods. “Some long mission or the other. You remember right, Amycus?”

“If you’re talking about the racing incident, then I remember alright. Vividly. In fact, it was in the air just a few streets away from here. I saw part of it from my window.”

Luca whistles. “I wish I could’ve seen it. I was out too, on a business trip. Only got back in time for the aftermath.”

Leifr frowns. “What exactly was *it*?”

“It, um, was basically a huge race,” Akio interjects. He’s finally managed to open the comic and pushes the tab along the counter to Amycus. He and Luca lean over it together. “On hoverboards. Hoverboard races were, uh pretty normal back then right, but they’d usually warn the locals and the businesses in that street and get permission and everything. But, uh, that time, a bunch of hoverboarders got really drunk and… they decided to just race. In the street. And, uh, because it was someone’s birthday, they wanted to make it interesting so… they raced around fifty feet in the air. I guess that’s what Mr. Amycus saw.”

The red-head snorts. “Just Amycus thanks. And yeah, it was pretty wild. A bunch of kids just wobbling all over the place at breakneck speeds, midair. I thought I was seeing things. Also this is pretty hilarious, good job kid.”

Akio’s face erupts in red. “Right! Thank you um. Where was I?”

“The drunk kids wanted to race in the air,” Leifr reminds him. The corner of his mouth twitch, and Akio promptly wishes for death for the nth time this evening.

“Um, right, yeah. So basically, one of them lost control of their board and fell, and they hit a passerby in the street. Both of them had to be rushed to the hospital. It turned out that the person who got hit was, uh, pretty important, and his family made a huge fuss. So the Architects banned the use of hoverboards anywhere in the Capital except for… well the back end of nowhere, pretty much.”

“Yeah and this comic is pretty much what happened after,” says Luca, sounding vastly entertained. “Except for a few details. Have you ever actually met the Warden in person? Because let me tell you, she does not think back on past crimes and laugh, holy shit. I’m not sure she actually laughs at all. This version of her is immensely preferrable. I demand you make it reality this *instant*.”

As Akio blue-screens over this mind-boggling statement, Leifr nods in thanks for the explanation, and gently nudges his friend aside to look at the comic. After a beat, a slow grin begins to curve his lips.

“Are you serious?” He asks. “I get that this is a parody, but did this really happen?”

“Except for a few details like he said,” Amycus chuckles. “I don’t remember anyone ever trying to sneak a hoverboard disguised as a giant rubber duck out of the wardens’ headquarters, for example, but it was only a little less ridiculous than that.” He pauses after a moment- he’s spotted someone a little further down waving their hand - they want a refill. “Sorry, I’ve got to go. Give me a minute.”

“How did they stop it?” Leifr asks as he leaves, no longer able to hold back his smile. Akio droops a bit, looking after the red-haired man and Luca snaps his fingers in front of his face- Akio comes back to himself with a jerk. “They couldn’t have repealed it? There haven’t been as many kids flying around for a while, now that I think about it.”

“Well they couldn’t,” he explains. “That person… could really have died so… They made designated areas and like aero-paths where it’s okay to fly. Mostly areas with less people. Like… air-traffic, I guess. So things died down after that.”

“That old lady must have been shaking with rage,” he  comments, leaning back in his seat. 

“Oh she was,” Luca chuckles. “I heard the wardens were trembling for days. Probably stung her pride, having to let them go, even a little.”

“She always did have an inflated ego,” Leifr notes, and Akio is in awe for a moment, remembering that these people have actually *met* legendary figures like the Warden. Probably *still* meet them. Regularly. *I’m not going to get in trouble for this right?*

“Ah but kid,” and Akio flinches just a little because the laughter has stopped and Luca’s voice has gone serious and a little quiet. “Are you planning on publishing this? Is the rest of your stuff like this? You’re going to draw attention to yourself, and not the fun kind.”

Akio blinks. He *has* considered publishing. It’s his dream. “I… it’s not that bad right? It portrays her in a positive light.”

“Does it?” Luca asks. Beside him, Leifr has stopped smiling too. “It’s an incident in which she lost face. Leifr just said it - she has one hell of an ego. She won’t care whether it was in a positive light or not. She’s not going to like it.”

“I- I mean… well-”

“You should listen to Luca,” Leifr murmurs. “I’m not as good with this kind of political maneuvering- but he’s not been wrong before.”

“But… it’s important,” Akio stammers. “It’s… it was a serious incident at the time and… and you’re right the wardens *did* mishandle it, just because the person involved was powerful. Luca turns his stare on him and it grows colder, just a little. Amycus returns it steadily. “If you want,” Amycus says, eyes still on Luca. “I can put you in touch with some friends of mine. They run a newspaper. Nothing big, just a few hundred khryos, but there you go.”

Akio…doesn’t answer. He has the sudden feeling that he’s lost control of the conversation, that what started with him showing off his art, has become something else. Something bigger. *You’re going to draw attention to yourself*, Luca had said. *And not the fun kind.*

Akio rubs his palms on his pants. They feel clammy, and cold in a way they haven’t been since Amycus cut him off and made him sit at the bar. Leifr still isn’t speaking, but he’s turned to Akio and is watching him steadily. Luca’s frowning hard. Akio looks up at the bartender. Amycus is looking at him. He’s put the washcloth down and is leaning against the bar, arms crossed. He’s waiting for Akio’s answer.

Akio ~~thinks~~ about his brothers, both Faction members, contributing to the Family. One of them has just been thanked by one of the most powerful, most decorated Families in the Empire. He ~~thinks~~ about his parents, about the disappointment in their eyes when they see him curled up in a corner with his drawing pad at a social event. He ~~thinks~~ about his peers, who aspire to be Vanguards, Wardens, Doctors, anything and everything except a pathetic, forgotten nobody.

He ~~thinks~~ about his mother, despairing, asking *Akio, can’t you do something that* matters *for once?*

He looks into Amycus’s eyes and knows, in that moment, that if he refuses, Amycus won’t bring it up again. That they can continue the conversation like this never happened. His fists clench, scrunching up the material of his pants.

“Yeah,” he says. “That’d be nice.”

These Councilors, publicly known as the Sovereign’s Advisors, execute orders, balance one another’s power, and guide national affairs. -OwWZsAqM_CiA6eyPUr9.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"you got lost alone during a field trip TENBY - KIM YI DEUN 9N","bold":true}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"That day, I lost my way. That day, the sky was so blue. And I was alone. The teacher and my friends were nowhere to be seen. All that was left for me was the blue sky. There was no one around, and all I could hear was the sound of my own footsteps. I sat down right there and looked up at the sky. I sat down right there and looked up at the endless blue sky. But I was not at peace. I was fear itself. I sat there without moving. I didn't run. I didn't even breathe. I just sat. Minutes passed. Maybe hours. I don't know. Then their voices — rough, angry, relieved all at once — cut through the silence. \"Where were you?!\" My friends crashed through the bushes, faces red, sweat dripping. They didn't ask if I was okay. They grabbed my arm and pulled. I stumbled. Almost fell. But they dragged me forward. Another step. Another. And the trip kept going. Like nothing happened. Like I hadn't just sat there becoming fear itself. I was sorry for my friends. Sorry that they had to find me like that. Sorry for the fear in their voices. And trip was so fun."}]}]

-OwQOgWMKFfrCBDIkvwy.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"The plot revolves around the horseman of Death, Death. 2500 years after the apocalypse was cancelled by God, the \"ultimate act of mercy\" he called it. The story follows Death, obsessed with destiny and purpose, putting the horsemen back together to rebel against God and create their own apocalypse on Earth. First he goes to Pestilence, who works at a company in Heaven. Heaven's companies are split into different sects, like catering to God, catering to humans, trade with other realms, etc. Pestilence works in the top human care company. Pestilence initially refuses to join Death, but after learning that the CEO of the company he works at is secretly Mammon, the fallen angel of Greed, Pestilence agrees on the condition that Death helps him out Mammon. Pestilence was the head of marketing at the company so he had access to it's social media accounts, they snuck into Mammon's office and live streamed him revealing himself, Heaven's paparazzi basically stormed the business and Mammon was sent back to Sheol by Archangel Michael. After that, since they didn't know where Famine was, they went to ask God, but visiting God is a very rare thing so Death called a favour from archangel Raphael and they were able to get in. God tells them only that Famine was in Sheol, Death and Pestilence said that they were doing reunion. God however, already knew their intentions, but did not stop them. Death and Pestilence use a train station called the World Tree Express to get to Sheol. A tv in the station explains that a long time ago, the Afterlife was an uncoordinated mess, and in the Norse world, Yggdrasil, the World Tree, was growing at an alarming rate. Soon even their universe wouldn't be able to contain it, so the Norse powers came together to unroot Yggdrasil and plant it into the bedrock of the very Afterlife itself; Limbo. The afterlives within would then collect on Yggdrasil, becoming it's leaves. The dwarves then, seeing this opportunity, built across the bark of the tree, allowing connection between the realms. Death and Pestilence snuck onto a train bound for Sheol. Sheol was the home of demons and fallen angels, Death and Pestilence arrived in the capital; Pandemonium, which was surprisingly civil. Death and Pestilence searched all throughout the city but couldn't find Famine. Then, a hooded stranger appeared and told the two horsemen that Famine was being held in the castle. Before Death and Pestilence could ask anymore questions, however, the stranger vanished. The castle, Satan's castle, was located in Hades (not the Greek one), Hades was the part of Sheol where sinful souls go to be tormented for eternity. Filled to the brim with pits of molten sulfur, which are filled to the brim with the tortured souls of sinners, feeling the agony of the lava burning their skin off only for it to grow back, all while mentally reliving the worst moments of their lives. Death and Pestilence walk to the castle, and into the throne room, in there was Satan. Well, it was part of him, he was a shadow on the wall, resembling a silhouette. Satan told the two he had no idea where Famine, but they didn't buy it. Once they left, they went into his prison cellar, where they found Famine. They broke Famine out but Satan was one step ahead of them, he released Hellspawn unto the three. Hellspawn, rabid fallen angels who lost their minds after the Fall. They managed to escape but Satan didn't pursue them, even though capturing Famine was the only guarantee he had that the End Times wouldn't occur, he still had other plans in mind. They then returned to Heaven to get War, who had joined Heaven's military after the Apocalypse was cancelled. They visited him and laid out their plan, although War cared deeply about the horsemen, he still didn't want them to do this. So, he let them go and hoped they chose not to. As the 3 were walking out of the building, a purple spark flew past Death. Death looked at where it was going and decided to chase after it. It eventually led him to a library where a Bible was laid out on a lectern. The verse that the spark landed on was Revelation 20:14: \"Then death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. The lake of fire is the second death.\" Death was, there are no words to describe his emotions. Betrayal? Hate? Sorrow? The story follows Death, obsessed with destiny and purpose, putting the horsemen back together to rebel against God and create their own apocalypse on Earth. First he goes to Pestilence, who works at a company in Heaven. Heaven's companies are split into different sects, like catering to God, catering to humans, trade with other realms, etc. Pestilence works in the top human care company. Pestilence initially refuses to join Death, but after learning that the CEO of the company he works at is secretly Mammon, the fallen angel of Greed, Pestilence agrees on the condition that Death helps him out Mammon. Pestilence was the head of marketing at the company so he had access to it's social media accounts, they snuck into Mammon's office and live streamed him revealing himself, Heaven's paparazzi basically stormed the business and Mammon was sent back to Sheol by Archangel Michael. After that, since they didn't know where Famine was, they went to ask God, but visiting God is a very rare thing so Death called a favour from archangel Raphael and they were able to get in. God tells them only that Famine was in Sheol, Death and Pestilence said that they were doing reunion. God however, already knew their intentions, but did not stop them. Death and Pestilence use a train station called the World Tree Express to get to Sheol. A tv in the station explains that a long time ago, the Afterlife was an uncoordinated mess, and in the Norse world, Yggdrasil, the World Tree, was growing at an alarming rate. Soon even their universe wouldn't be able to contain it, so the Norse powers came together to unroot Yggdrasil and plant it into the bedrock of the very Afterlife itself; Limbo. The afterlives within would then collect on Yggdrasil, becoming it's leaves. The dwarves then, seeing this opportunity, built across the bark of the tree, allowing connection between the realms. Before Death and Pestilence could ask anymore questions, however, the stranger vanished. The castle, Satan's castle, was located in Hades (not the Greek one), Hades was the part of Sheol where sinful souls go to be tormented for eternity. Filled to the brim with pits of molten sulfur, which are filled to the brim with the tortured souls of sinners, feeling the agony of the lava burning their skin off only for it to grow back, all while mentally reliving the worst moments of their lives. Death and Pestilence walk to the castle, and into the throne room, in there was Satan. Well, it was part of him, he was a shadow on the wall, resembling a silhouette. Satan told the two he had no idea where Famine, but they didn't buy it. Once they left, they went into his prison cellar, where they found Famine. They broke Famine out but Satan was one step ahead of them, he released Hellspawn unto the three. Hellspawn, rabid fallen angels who lost their minds after the Fall. They managed to escape but Satan didn't pursue them, even though capturing Famine was the only guarantee he had that the End Times wouldn't occur, he still had other plans in mind. They then returned to Heaven to get War, who had joined Heaven's military after the Apocalypse was cancelled. They visited him and laid out their plan, although War cared deeply about the horsemen, he still didn't want them to do this. So, he let them go and hoped they chose not to. As the 3 were walking out of the building, a purple spark flew past Death. Death looked at where it was going and decided to chase after it. It eventually led him to a library where a Bible was laid out on a lectern. The verse that the spark landed on was Revelation 20:14: "Then death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. The lake of fire is the second death." Death was, there are no words to describe his emotions. Betrayal? Hate? Sorrow? He didn't know himself, all he did know was that this would only motivate him even more to fulfill his destiny. Death turned around and instead of the other two horsemen, he saw his scythe. They entered and suddenly it got foggy and the group was seperated. War found someone crouching in the corner but was attacked. Then, as Death was trying to figure a way out, getting annoyed instead of scared, War showed up, but he was acting strange, different. Then the two found Famine and Pestilence. War, suddenly ran away deeper into the house, the group chased after him, Death getting even more mad. Eventually, War ed them into the basement where they saw a mound of apparitions collected on the ceiling, watching them. War has blue eyes now. Death recognized the apparitions as poltergeists, but a special kind of poltergeist, these ghosts were never able to move on, and through immense willpower, they were able to force themselves into the afterlife. Now the only way they can leave is for them to enter a body and walk out, so sometimes multiple poltergeists form alliances and possess and individual host together, which was what happened to War. War explained that there was no escape and they should just give up. But then, Death burst into purple flames and raised his scythe, commanding the spirits out of the Death and the ceiling, using the power he was able to force the spirits into Hades. Death, exhausted from the display, passed out. He then woke up in the carriage, War also recovering. The next day, we focus on Sheol. And into the life of someone new, the daughter of Satan; Michelle. Michelle lived a relatively normal life, except for the fact that no one talked to her except for one friend because her father was literally Satan, even demons and fallen angels fear him. Michelle even had a crush, but he wasn't the average jock popular boy, he actually kept to himself quite often, his interests being accounting and drawing. He was pretty mundane and that's why Michelle liked him. Michelle and her best friend spend the next few days getting everything she needs for prom, and the courage to ask out her crush. All while hiding it from her father, who would never let her do anything like this. Eventually she gets everything and asks him out and he says yes. She has an amazing time and people even started talking to her more. But when she came back home, she was called into her father's throne room, there was the head of her date on a pike, his blood pooling down the wood. Satan said that if she ever went behind her back again, he would personally see to it that she regret that forever. Michelle runs to her room and finds a small device. She takes it an d presses it and puts it on the floor, it then shows a hologram of archangel Michael, Michelle says she ready to talk. Focus back on the horsemen, its night in the garden and they're resting. Death is sitting outside, staring at his scythe, when a bright light comes from the forest, and steps through. A glowing woman. Death regards her as Life. Life and Death catch up a bit, Life always did prefer to talk to him over the Grim Reaper. Life says she's worried about Death but Death dismisses her. Life tells Death to let go of the scythe but he refuses. After a rise in more tension, they fight. It ends in a stalemate, but Life walks away, but not before telling Death that he's going down a dark path. Michelle tells Michael about her father's plans; plans to invade Heaven. But before he finish, guard barge into her room and drag her out, Michael saying her sacrifice was for the greater good. The guards bring her to Satan who banishes her from Sheol. She gets on a World Tree Train bound for Asgard. Satan watches, a flicker of blue sparkles in his eyes before he brushes himself off and it fades away. Death and the horsemen make it to the station and they board a train. They make it to Asgard, where they intended to discuss their plans further because they couldn't do that in Heaven. But they are stopped by Heimdall, they are almost sent back to Heaven when they are saved by Michell. Michelle tellls them that they owe her and they need to help her stop her father, they reluctantly agree. Satan sends scientists to earth to get the blood of Jesus, which they use to restore Satan to his body. Satan gathers his army outside his castle but then the horsemen show up. Satan turns into a dragon and fights them. Death bursts into purple flames and tries to attack Satan but gets knocked unconcsious. Death meets Life in his mind and together Death learns to overcome his obsession with destiny. They beat Satan, and then heaven's army arrives and defeats Satan's army and Satan is banished to Limbo.

-OwWUy7NzyNuR6WAm7Cb.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"The missed call from 'Mom' glowed on his lock screen for twelve seconds before he swiped it away and stepped into his car. He finally pulled into the parking lot with only 10 minutes until his flight leaves however a grimy hand clamped onto his sleeve just before the revolving doors, and he turned to find a homeless man's bloodshot eyes fixed on his own. 'That plane's carrying ghosts,' the homeless man rasped, but he yanked his arm free and pushed through the door, deaf to the warning buried beneath the terminal's roar. The homeless man lunged, grabbing his coat. He shoved hard, stumbled, then sprinted. At the gate, the desk agent was already locking the door. \"Sorry, sir, doors are closed.\" Planes always leave without you. This one felt different. He kicks the door open, tossing his keys onto the counter. He was pissed, he was so close but the homeless man didn't know how to mind his own business. Hours pass in a haze of takeout and TV. Then the news anchors eyes meet his: \"breaking updates on flight 237—no survivors.\" The remote slips from his hand, his eyes go wide, that was his flight. He stared at the screen. The homeless man's words echoed: \"That plane's carrying ghosts.\" It wasn't madness. It was a warning. He grabbed his coat, heart pounding. He had to find him. He gets into his car speeding along the highway the same way he did this morning, but this time's different. He wasn't rushing to catch a flight, he was rushing to thank a man he ignored. He reached the same parking lot he encountered the homeless man, but he wasn't there. He searched every street corner, every alley. Nothing. The man had vanished like smoke. Standing in the rain, he finally understood—some warnings arrive once, carried by voices we're too busy to hear. He vowed never to ignore another. He steps in his car, still soaking wet and drives away, on the way home he saw a dark silhouette in the rain. He got out to check, it was someone on the edge of a bridge. He approached slowly, the way you'd approach a wounded animal. \"I don't know what you're carrying,\" he said, \"but I've learned you can't outrun it.\" The suicidal man's voice cracked: \"I lost everything. Job. Wife. Reason to get up.\" He stared at the water. \"Why should I stay?\" The man stepped closer. \"Because tomorrow you might save someone. I almost got on a plane that crashed. I'm here because someone tried to warn me.\" He just listened. After an hour, the man stepped back from the edge. He walked home with a strange lightness in his chest. The pride felt good, but it faded fast—replaced by a quieter ache. He pulled out his phone, staring at his mom's contact. Three years of silence. He hit call before he could talk himself out of it. \"Hello?\" Her voice was smaller than he remembered. He opened his mouth, but the words tangled. \"Mom... I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.\" Silence stretched. Then, a shaky breath. \"I've been waiting three years to hear you say that. Come home, sweetheart.\" He hung up, tears streaming, feeling lighter than he had in years. As soon as the words came out he drove to her house, the same place he hasn't seen in years. He stood outside her door, hand hovering over the handle. When she opened it, her hair was grayer, her eyes softer. She didn't say a word—just pulled him into an embrace that smelled like lavender and forgiveness. \"I made your favorite,\" she whispered. \"Chicken soup.\" For the first time in years, he felt like he was finally where he belonged."}]}]

-OwVVK5d1ZyjQ0mkNL-W.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Last Monday, I had an unforgettable experience when I missed the school bus and arrived late for class. It was a lesson that I will always remember."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"That morning, I woke up much later than usual because I forgot to set my alarm clock. When I looked at the time, I jumped out of bed in panic. I quickly brushed my teeth, took a shower, put on my school uniform, and packed my school bag. I skipped breakfast because I did not want to waste any more time."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"I ran as fast as I could to the bus stop. Unfortunately, just as I reached it, I saw the school bus driving away. I shouted and waved my hands, hoping the driver would stop, but it was too late. I felt upset and worried because I knew I would be late for school."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"I immediately called my father for help. Luckily, he was still at home and agreed to drive me to school. However, the roads were crowded with morning traffic, and we had to stop at several red traffic lights. I kept looking at my watch and became more nervous with every passing minute."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"When we finally arrived at school, the first lesson had already begun. I hurried to my classroom, took a deep breath, and knocked gently on the door. My teacher looked at me and asked why I was late. I politely explained that I had missed the school bus after waking up late. My teacher accepted my explanation but reminded me that punctuality is very important. I apologized to my teacher and quietly took my seat."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Although I felt embarrassed, I paid close attention to the lesson and borrowed my friend's notes to catch up. That day taught me a valuable lesson about responsibility and good time management. Since then, I have made it a habit to prepare my school bag the night before and set two alarm clocks. I have never missed the school bus again."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]}]

We thought a bad weather just occurred, but it was a Cataclysmic storm about to come to our path, not only did a storm appear but an hurricane, a thunderous roar gave us goosebumps. From the outside view, i see people running for their lives but caught up to them and it destroyed cities laying them into dust, it was too late to evacuate but we can find shelter to avoid them. The way we can survive a hurricane is to go as down as possible. All of a sudden, it stopped and the storm didn't come back that night, but the silence it left behind was worse. Huddled in the cracked shell of a library, the survivors listened for wind, for thunder, for anything. But there were only the drip of water and the slow groan of settling rubble. No one said it aloud, but they all knew: the stillness felt like waiting. The storm returned at dawn, a wall of black wind howling through the shattered streets. The survivors pressed themselves into the library's basement, clutching pipes and each other as the building groaned above them. Glass shattered. Concrete cracked. But the foundation held. When the wind finally passed and the dust settled, they emerged bloodied, deafened, but alive into a world that still demanded they fight for it. While the storm raged above, one of them noticed something the wind never touched the copper pipes running through the basement. They traced the pattern, realizing the storm swerved around metal. Before the next surge hit, they pieced it together: the storm hated electricity. They scrambled to reroute exposed wires, weaving a cage of current around their shelter. The storm retreated, screaming, and they finally understood what could stop it just as the horizon darkened, signaling its departure for the next town. They didn't waste time celebrating. The storm was already crawling toward the next valley, and somewhere out there, another town had no idea what was coming. Someone found an old ham radio in the rubble. They patched it together, and through the static, a voice answered. \"We see it on radar,\" the voice said. \"But we don't know how to stop it.\" The survivors looked at each other, knowing exactly what to say next. The last storm never reached the next town. They called ahead—explained the copper, the electricity, the cage of wire. Every town from there learned, adapted, passed it on. Years later, storms still came, but they were met with humming metal towers and defiant lights. The Storm That Healed
A storm arrives carrying more than just rain.
Dark clouds cover the sky. Thunder rolls far away. Soon, heavy rain starts to fall. It beats hard against the windows and streets.
Lynn sits by the window alone. For many days, she has felt sad and tired. Small troubles and worries make her upset. She stays away from friends and quiets herself down, thinking the dark mood will never leave.
Strong wind shakes the old tree in the street. Its leaves are bent by the storm, but the tree still stands straight. Rain washes off the dirt on every leaf and stone.
Watching the rain, Lynn slowly calms down.
She understands that storms are not only bad.
They clean the dirty air, wash away tiredness, and let everything start fresh.
Slowly, thunder stops. The heavy rain turns into light drizzle. Dark clouds move away, and the sky becomes clear again. Cool wind blows in, bringing the fresh smell of grass and wet earth.
Lynn takes a deep breath.
This storm brought more than rain.
It brought peace and hope. It washed away her sadness and gave her a new start.
After the storm, everything looks bright again.
-----------
The Storm That Healed
A storm arrives carrying more than just rain.
Dark clouds roll across the pale evening sky, swallowing the last trace of sunlight. Thunder rumbles in the distance, low and heavy, before the downpour crashes down upon the quiet town. The rain pounds against rooftops and windows, washing over every dusty corner of the streets.
Lynn sits alone by the window, staring blankly outside. For weeks, her heart has been tangled in quiet sorrows. Disappointments, unspoken worries, and endless self-doubt have weighed her down, turning her days gray and lifeless. She has isolated herself from noise and company, believing the dullness inside her would never fade.
The wind howls and shakes the branches of the old tree standing in the alley. Its leaves are violently tossed and bent by the storm, yet the trunk remains steady, rooted firmly in the ground. Rain pours relentlessly, cleaning every leaf, every stone, every speck of dirt that has gathered through days of heat and stillness.
As Lynn watches, her tight chest slowly loosens.
She realizes storms are not only destructive.
They wash away dust. They clear the heavy air. They break stagnation and make room for new growth.
Through the chaotic rain, she sees calm hidden within the wildness. The world does not end in a storm—it resets. It breathes again.
Gradually, the thunder fades. The fierce rain softens into a gentle drizzle. The dark clouds drift apart, revealing a clean, quiet sky. Fresh wind blows through the open window, carrying the pure scent of wet soil and green leaves.
Lynn closes her eyes and takes a deep breath.
This storm brought more than rain.
It brought clarity. It brought release. It washed away her lingering despair and gave her heart a quiet, gentle restart.
When she opens her eyes again, everything feels lighter. The world looks brighter, softer, and full of silent hope.
After the storm, everything begins anew

The Rain That Changed Everything
A storm arrives carrying more than just rain.
The sky turned grey in only a few minutes. Wind rushed through the empty streets, and then the rain came down hard.
Noah sat alone in his small room.
He had been feeling lost for a long time. He tried his best, but nothing seemed to go right. He felt tired, lonely, and stuck inside his own sad thoughts.
He stared outside at the storm.
The trees shook wildly. The world looked cold and messy. But as he watched, he noticed something strange.
The rain cleaned everything.
It washed the dust off the roads. It cleaned the dark, dirty leaves. It made the whole town look new again.
Slowly, the storm became softer.
The loud thunder faded away. The heavy rain turned into quiet drops. The air outside felt cool, clean, and peaceful.
Noah finally stood up.
He realized storms were not only scary.
Sometimes the hardest moments in life are like this rain. They come loud and sudden, and they break everything old. But they also clear the way for something better.
This storm brought more than rain.
It brought a quiet chance to start over.
When the sun softly peeked out of the clouds, Noah smiled.
For the first time in a long while, he felt hope again.

More Than Rain

Jake had been feeling stuck for a long time. Small troubles kept piling up, and he lost his passion for the things he once loved. Every day felt dull and gray, and he could not find a way out of his low mood.

The rain washed dust from the roads and refreshed the dry trees. The whole world looked clean and bright after being soaked. As he watched, the heavy weight in his heart slowly lifted.
He realized storms were not just scary. They washed away tiredness and cleared the stale air. Hard times in life were just like this storm. Though painful at first, they could sweep away confusion and bring a new start.
Soon the rain stopped. The sun peeked through the clouds, and a faint rainbow appeared in the sky. The fresh wind carried the sweet smell of grass.
This storm brought more than rain.
It brought hope and courage.
Jake took a deep breath, and made up his mind to face life with a new attitude.

-OwRJttpCWHthSbLlMtd.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"I went on a school trip once, and I got lost. It was in the morning, I was prepared to go out, happily with all my friends, then, we departed, we were joking around and having fun on the bus. An hour later, we arrived. It was a field trip, a trip to explore the forest. The forest was quite dark and scary, but we had our friends, so it was better. A while later we all sat down and ate lunch. After I finished, I saw something in the forest, I got curious and went towards it. When I came back, everyone was gone. When the last voice faded into the trees, I didn't move at first. I waited for a joke, for someone to call my name. But the forest only swallowed the silence whole and left me standing in it alone. For a while I was relieved to be free of the group's noise and pressure. For a few minutes, the solitude felt like a gift. Then the sun dropped, and the gift turned into a cage. I was stretching my legs, taking a deep breath, smiling to myself. But then the absence hit — no footsteps behind me, no voices calling ahead. My relief curdled into dread. I was lost, it was dark, and the only sound was my own heartbeat. Then — a twig snapped nearby. Not an animal, but something that sounded like it walked on two feet. I froze. Heart pounding, breathing shallow. The snapped twig was followed by another, then a low whistle — a simple tune, out of place in the dark. There was a shadow, that's all I needed to keep running. The shadow wasn't chasing, just standing there motionless. After hours of alien, twisting woods, my foot hit a familiar root. The shape of it, the way the ground sloped here — I knew this spot. I stopped. My heart, which had been pounding with fear, now hammered with something else — hope, maybe. I didn't trust it. I listened, waiting for the forest to trick me, for the whistling to start again. But there was only silence. Then, a voice. Not the pursuer's tune, but a shout. A name. My name. I opened my mouth. At first, nothing came out — my throat was raw from holding back fear. But then I shouted, voice cracking: \"Here! I'm here!\" Branches rustled. A figure emerged from the darkness. It was my teacher. The man looked pale, exhausted. He had been searching all night. For a long moment, neither of us spoke. Then my teacher said, \"You're alive.\" And we all went on the bus and got home safely."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]}]

MElwPCsZEaaqKQAeCOXeM4qWdYu1.summary:
**Why Human Creativity Still Matters in the Age of AI** Artificial intelligence has made remarkable strides in recent years. From generating realistic images to composing music and writing essays, AI systems can now produce content that once required significant human effort. However, despite these advances, the rise of AI-generated content—sometimes dismissively called "AI slop"—raises important questions about the value of human creativity. First, human creativity is inherently tied to lived experience. When a person writes a story, paints a picture, or composes a song, they draw upon emotions, memories, and perspectives that no algorithm can truly replicate. AI may mimic patterns, but it does not feel joy, sorrow, or nostalgia. It does not know what it means to love, to lose, or to hope. These elements give human art its depth and authenticity. Second, human creativity involves intention and meaning. A writer chooses each word deliberately, considering tone, audience, and purpose. An AI, by contrast, generates text based on statistical probabilities. It does not understand what it is saying. It has no message to convey, no truth to express. The result may look convincing, but it lacks the soul of genuine communication. Third, creativity is a process, not just a product. The struggle to find the right word, the the right phrase, the moment of breakthrough after hours of frustration—these experiences shape the creator and give the final work its meaning. AI bypasses this entirely. It offers a shortcut, but shortcuts often lead to shallow destinations. Moreover, human creativity fosters connection. When we read a poem or hear a story, we connect with another person's inner world. We recognize shared feelings, struggles, and triumphs. AI-generated content may entertain, but it rarely moves us in the same way. We know, deep down, that no one was truly behind the words. And that matters. This is not to say AI has no place in creative work. It can be a useful tool for brainstorming, overcoming writer's block, or generating rough drafts. But it should remain a tool, not a replacement. The moment we outsource our creativity entirely to machines, we lose something essential about what it means to be human. In conclusion, while AI continues to improve, human creativity remains irreplaceable. Our experiences, our intentions, our struggles, and our connections give art its power. So before dismissing creative work as "AI slop," remember: behind every meaningful piece of art, there is a person who chose to create it. And that choice is something no algorithm can ever truly make.
-----------
The old wooden bridge stretched across the river like a forgotten memory. Every afternoon after school, sixteen-year-old Ethan crossed it on his way home. The bridge was quiet, surrounded by tall trees and the gentle sound of flowing water. Although the villagers often warned that the bridge was old and unsafe, Ethan never gave their words much thought. To him, it was simply the shortest path home.
 
One rainy afternoon, dark clouds gathered overhead as Ethan hurried across the bridge. Halfway through, he noticed a frightened golden retriever trapped between two broken planks. The dog whined desperately, unable to free itself. Ethan looked around, but there was no one nearby. Thunder echoed through the valley, and the river below surged with the heavy rain. He knew that staying on the bridge was dangerous, yet leaving the helpless animal behind felt impossible.
 
Carefully, Ethan placed his backpack on the ground and crawled toward the dog. Each step made the wooden boards creak louder. The frightened dog struggled even harder, causing the bridge to shake. Ethan spoke softly to calm it while reaching for its collar. Just as his fingers touched the leash, a loud crack rang through the air. One of the support beams beneath the bridge snapped. Ethan's heart raced as the bridge tilted slightly. Fear urged him to run, but determination kept him moving. With all his strength, he pulled the dog free from the broken planks.
 
At that very moment, another section of the bridge collapsed behind them. Ethan grabbed the dog and sprinted toward the riverbank. The remaining boards swayed beneath his feet, threatening to give way at any second. Finally, with one desperate leap, he landed safely on solid ground. Seconds later, the center of the bridge crashed into the roaring river below. Ethan collapsed onto the wet grass, breathing heavily while the grateful dog licked his face. Relief replaced the fear that had filled him only moments before.
 
The dog's owner soon arrived after searching the nearby trails. Overjoyed to find his pet safe, he thanked Ethan repeatedly and brought him back to the village. News of Ethan's bravery spread quickly. Although many praised him for risking his life, Ethan admitted that he had simply done what he believed was right. The village council decided to replace the dangerous bridge with a stronger one, ensuring that no one else would face the same danger.
 
Months later, Ethan stood on the newly built bridge and watched the river flow peacefully beneath him. He realized that courage was not the absence of fear but the decision to act despite it. The experience had changed him forever, teaching him that even ordinary people can make extraordinary choices when compassion guides their actions. As the sun set behind the hills, Ethan smiled, knowing that one act of kindness had not only saved a life but had also inspired an entire community to create a safer future.

As the days went by, and as the wind blew through his sail, he could only watch as the only flicker of memoria he had left drifted away."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Though the ocean was vast, it was lonely. The sailor could only listen to the sound of calm waves as it carried him further from his home -- a contrast to the turmoil that brewed inside him. The moonlight luminated onto his face, such beauty, but he only wanted to hide from its radiant susceptibility that shone onto his figurative memorandum of confidentiality. It felt too bright. As if it was carving every crevice of his skin to expose the regret and guilt that lingered beneath. The inevitable remorse that emerged after the act of abandonment."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"He stared into his dim reflection in the water, the liquid failing to capture the exact features of his face as it swashed and warped. He pitied himself, he cried to himself and he wanted to gain control of himself. "}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"He was like the seasons that came and went. -OwQAUr-5ry0NA0KQugI.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Leo is a burned-out remote worker who hasn't left their apartment in days. At 3 AM, they collapse into bed and fall into a deep sleep. They wake to find their gray apartment transformed: glowing ivy on the walls, a starry sky where the ceiling should be, and their familiar city street now alive with impossible creatures — goblins in business suits, carriages pulled by smoke, street lamps held by floating spirits. A silver-eyed woman named Seraphine appears at their door. \"You've been asleep a long time, Leo. Welcome to the real world. \"Seraphine explains the truth: a magical world has always existed alongside the mundane one, hidden by a barrier called the Veil. Leo's exhaustion wasn't burnout — their mind was breaking through the filter. They are a \"Walker,\" a rare human who can exist in both worlds. Leo finds refuge in a sanctuary with other Awakened. They train under Mira, a witch; Kael, a fee; and Thorn, a fellow human. But the Veil is thinning dangerously. The culprit is Marcus Chen, Leo's former mentor, who wants to tear the Veil down completely — believing humans deserve the truth, even if it destroys them. The Veil Keepers, who protect the barrier, hunt Leo as a threat. Hunted by both sides, Leo hits a low point on a rooftop. Kael tells them: \"The world doesn't care if you give up. But if you fight, you can make it spin the way you want. \"Marcus's ritual begins at the city's heart — a clock tower where the Veil is being torn open. The sky splits, showing both worlds overlapping. Battle erupts around Leo as allies and enemies clash. Leo phases through the chaos and reaches Marcus at the center of the vortex. Instead of attacking, Leo offers a third path: not destroying the Veil, not reinforcing it, but reshaping it into a permeable threshold that opens only for those who are ready. Leo steps into the vortex, feels the Veil tearing around them, and uses their Walker power to transform it. The sky mends. The ritual collapses. The word Changed, the Veil becomes a gentle doorway, not a wall or open gate. Suddenly Marcus disappears.... After that they found out Veil Keepers adapt Marcus. Month later, Leo stands on a rooftop at sunset. The city below is alive with quiet wonder — a child chasing a firefly, a couple near singing roses, shadows that move a little strangely. The two worlds are learning to coexist. Imperfectly. Beautifully. Seraphine, Mira, Kael, and Thorn call Leo down for dinner. As Leo turns away, they catch their reflection in a window. For the first time in years, they recognize themselves. They are no longer tired. They are awake."}]}]

-OwQG5001yiUt_uit_fy.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Twenty years ago. It wasn't appeared. When I was growing up, AI was something in movies — robots with feelings, computers that took over the world. Now I carry AI in my pocket. It helps me write emails, find information, and even generate pictures."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"And that's what strikes me most. How ordinary it has become. We've gotten so used to AI doing impressive things that we barely stop to notice anymore. A program that can write a poem? Cool, but have you seen the new update? A machine that can diagnose illness better than a doctor? Interesting, but what's for lunch? We've absorbed this massive change into our daily lives without really sitting with what is mean. And I think about all the data that goes into training these systems. Every word I've ever typed, every search I've ever made, every video I've ever watched — it's all part of that AI learns from. Not just me, either. Billions of people. The whole internet. All of human knowledge and conversation, boiled down into patterns and probabilities. And from that , something emerges that can talk back to us like a person."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"That's incredible. And also a little weird. But it doesn't understand what it's saying. It's more like a really good mimic. It's seen so many examples of human writing that it knows what words usually come next. It's a prediction machine dressed up as a conversation partner."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Here's another thing I've been thinking about. When AI writes a poem or paints a picture, who made it? The AI? The people who built it? The millions of artists whose work it learned from? Or no one at all? I don't have a good answer for that either. But I think it matters. Because creativity has always been one of those things that felt deeply, unmistakably human. And now the machine can do it too. Not as well, maybe. But well enough that you have to stop and check."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"I watched a video once of someone asking an AI to write a love letter. The letter was beautiful. Full of longing and tenderness. The person reading it started crying. That got to me. Because the AI didn't feel any of that. It just knew which words fit together to make someone else feel something. And that made me wonder: does it matter if the feeling is real if the result is real? If a machine writes something that makes you cry, does it matter that the machine didn't cry?"}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"I don't know. But I keep coming back to that question. Maybe that's what this whole reflection is about. Not understanding AI, but understanding ourselves through it. Every new development in AI holds up a mirror and asks: what do you value? What makes you you? What are you afraid of losing? What are you excited to gain? The answers change depending on the day, depending on my mood, depending on whether I just watched something amazing or something scary. And maybe that's the point. The development of AI isn't a straight line. It's not going from bad to good or from simple to complex. It's a messy, complicated, human story. "}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]}]

-OwQ9Cbqn-JO7SAiF7o_.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Josh was... let's say, big bodied. In fact, calling him that would be describing the Atlantic Ocean as a cup of water. However, he actually had a six-pack in grade 1. Ok, yeah, it was six packs of happy meals. The point is that people called him names, but he used to tune them out all the time. No one liked him in the first place, even before he became, well, as his friends called him, a 'big back'. He ate all kinds of food at home, and, despite what most people think of fat guys, he actually ate his vegetables. He just ate too many burgers from the McDonalds down the street."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"However, as he entered 7th grade, he felt uneasy. He started to notice how his classmates distanced themselves from him. What made it worse was that there was a daddy-long-legs of doubt (or cellar spider of doubt if you prefer to be not freaky) growing in his head. And every day, he could hear it whisper unkind comments. Every time he bit down on a juicy whopper from Burger King, he could hear the voice of doubt in his mind. The voice was not really 'a voice' but really the disembodied sounds of his classmates' insults. What was important was that it shook him. The feeling of being shaken was like shaking a milkshake, then stirring it. If you want to know how that feels like, hop into an un-shaken milkshake and see for yourself."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Anyway, Josh had no choice but to live with the consequences of his actions. However, as he grew, a kinder voice whispered into Josh's ear. It said \"you are capable of change, Josh. I believe in you.\" And let's be real, Josh did not believe himself until that point. But as the voice kept encouraging him, the daddy-long-legs of doubt retreated back into its little hidey-hole. Josh now believed in himself. He could change. At least, that's what his classmates didn't say about him. As he ate less whoppers, samurai burgers and Kentucky fried chicken wings, he became thinner, and when he graduated from college, he actually had a six-pack (value bundle of mineral water bottles). Nevertheless, he changed, like the guiding voice in his head said. And now, he was ready to face the world, not as a \"stinky big back\" but as Josh. Finally, he could live as himself and not an insulting label about what he looks like from the outside."}]}]

-OwRMw9kfRV1b_vvSRLw.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"There was a sailor that spent most of his time away from its family. He had no time at all to be with his family because he had to work constantly in order to meet and provide basic needs. While he sails across the sea he usually sings a song that reminds him of his family. He usually sings it when he feels lonely or when he just misses them. One day when he was feeling extremely exhausted, he was barely able to stay awake and do his job. This was due to lack of rest and also how much he had missed his family. He was so down that he didn't want sing the song that would always cheer him up until something magical had happened . As each wave passed by he heard each verse coming from it. It was almost as if the ocean was singing to him live and reminding him that he was never alone . The sailor was full of emotions and took it as a sign to not give up and continue the journey . As he continued forward he felt sprays of water pat his back as if it was family member. While sailing he had found a bottle containing a piece of paper floating towards him. This was the exact paper that his family had wrote for him a few years ago that went missing. He was shocked and amazed. He read the letter and received the strength to push on and reach his destination.   This was a moment that he would never forget."}]}]

-OwVQCYFBcH1WCQ-KAvw.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"A life that was never meant for me. A fate that I still preserve today. I was nothing but a dull piece of life in society. My name is Adam, cliche huh? Well that's because it's not my real name, I made it myself. My parents were separated when I was 2, and despite being 24 now, I still rely on the donated food given out by the adoption center. I have nothing. No degree, no home, no parents, just my soul running on the rock-hard soil above my feet & a Nokia phone."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Months pass by, with not even a single conversation with human life. A man with a suit & tie walked up to me and whispered in my ears \"Meet me next week, 19th June, at the Bro-cheers & Co. factory, two blocks across this road. I can get you off of this road\" My eyes gleamed with excitement. For once, i had a taste of victory at the palm of my hands. Something had clicked into my life without me even trying. \"But make it fast, at 9:00AM sharp.\" I rushed to the saloon to get my $1 haircut, with a secondhand suit nearby."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"A day before my meet-up, I called my adoption center, telling them i don't need them anymore. I rushed to the printing center to print a 1-page resume made on my Nokia, which was made up of fake professions & experiences of volunteering events. I made sure to set my alarm as early as possible, with 5 separate alarm clocks ranging from 1AM to 5AM."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\""},{"text":"DRINGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGG,\" ","italic":true},{"text":"the alarms went loud in my ears, like a calling from hell. I rush across the road with my wrinkled suit, only to find out that I was accompanied with fussy neighbors who hated my alarms. The neighborhood rushed to me as if they were having a protest, as I try to hurdle across the crowd. After crawling through a elderly's legs, i escaped my cage and ran straight to the company building. A minute before 9, I ran straight across the river, with my eyes seeing the building. Then, a bump into a pillar. I fell into the river along with my resume & my Nokia phone... I laid on the riverbed."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\"ADAM! Someone please get him some help...\" My eyes flickered on and off. There I was in the hospital bed, with broken bones & a fractured tooth. I never knew how could've I ever return from this. The police came in and gave a thorough report to me."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\"Your name is.... Adam, right?\""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\"Yes.\""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\"You're lucky you fell into that river, we discovered that the company was going to kidnap you if you went.\""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"\"WHAT?!?\""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]}]

-OwQE1vE4KRjEdq6yjfO.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Charlotte was born ordinary. By seven years old , she could read at a high school level. By eight years old , she solved problems her teachers couldn't. By nine years old , she played three instruments by ear. Everyone called her a prodigy. No one called her lonely. Her mother, Althea, whispered to her every night: \"You are special, my love. The most special girl in the world.\" Charlotte believed her. But late at night, she wondered: If I can do anything, why can't I make friends? The other children stared at her like a creature in a glass box. She answered questions before they were finished. She corrected teachers without meaning to. Slowly, loneliness became a second skin."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"When Charlotte was eleven, a girl named Maya arrived — crooked teeth, wild curls, unbothered by mockery. She sat with Charlotte at lunch. She didn't care about the genius. She cared about the girl who liked honey in her tea. For two years, Charlotte was happy."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"It all changed when Maya went to Charlotte's house for a sleepover. That was the first time Maya met both of Charlotte's parents. Charlotte's parents were very kind to her friend Maya. Charlotte said her parents were the best parents in the world. Maya thought that way too. Charlotte and Maya played happily in Charlotte's room. Althea came to their room and said, \"It's time to sleep, children,\" and she turned off the light."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"When Charlotte fell asleep, Maya woke up and went to the toilet. When she passed by Charlotte's parents' room, she heard a conversation she was not supposed to hear. The message she heard was that Charlotte's parents had cursed their own daughter. If Charlotte made a true friend, she could not be a genius anymore — only an ordinary person. And now her parents were scared that if Charlotte actually made a true friend, their daughter could not be a genius anymore."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Maya told this to Charlotte. Charlotte eventually believed Maya. The only way to break the curse was for Charlotte to choose to lose her genius. She stood before her parents and said: \"I'd rather be ordinary and have Maya than be a genius and be alone.\""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"Her genius faded. She became an ordinary girl. But she smiled for the first time in years. Even though Charlotte was not a genius anymore, she was still smart and happy. That is how Charlotte's life is now."}]}]

-OwRKrzumvnGBP5bbJjz.content: [{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"My older sister had always lied to me, until she couldn't resist but tell the truth to me. It all started since when we were very young. My sister would always have a quarrel with me and lie to our parents that I started it first. She was also very suspicious as she couldn't reveal the truth whenever I question her about literally anything. Such as \"Have you finished your homework?\" or \"Have you done your chores?\" and she would just answer me a response like \"Maybe\" or \"Sure\", but I already knew that she was completely lying to me on mostly everything. And on one day, there was a VERY big project that I had to submit. To apply context, my teacher gave us a project to do, and it was an individual project and that she gave us a few weeks to do it. My project was simple. It was to build a rocket ship using sustainable materials. I spent the rest of the week trying to perfect the rocket ship, by even decorating it. On the morning of the submission day however, my rocket ship had strangely disappeared during the night. After the realization hit me, I began to feel anxious and worried, so I went and asked my sister if she had seen it. And to no one's surprise, she says that she hasn't seen it. Although I trusted her response was believable enough, I could not but feel suspicious of her that day. So I went into school bare-handed, and got a straight zero for my project. Back at home, she giggled at me as she hid the rocket ship under our house's basement. Though I was not too angry or sad about it, I casually shrugged it off."}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":""}]},{"type":"paragraph","children":[{"text":"In the present day, we were both now working adults. Last week, my sister texted me, saying that our grandmother had passed away. For context, I loved my grandmother very much and cared deeply for her. So I thought it would be fake and that she wanted me to feel sad. But this time, there was a feeling where she wasn't lying. Because it was. My sister called and cried on the call, suddenly feeling deep regret and promises to not lie to me ever again. However, I do not know why she would apologize to me at this moment where our grandmother had passed away, but I suspect it was because that our grandmother's passing had affected my sister's feelings. And that our grandmother also tells us to not lie."}]}]
